section.title: Parables of Prayer and the Rich Ruler
section.sectionRationale: Jesus teaches persistent prayer through a widow who wears down an unjust judge, and true prayer through a tax collector who simply begs for mercy and goes home justified while the proud Pharisee does not. He welcomes little children as the pattern of the kingdom, then watches a rich ruler turn away sorrowful, for it is easier for a camel to pass through a needle's eye than for the rich to enter, though what is impossible with man is possible with God. He foretells His passion a third time, and a blind beggar who will not be silenced receives his sight and follows.
section.thesis: The kingdom is entered not by the self-assured but by those who pray without losing heart, cry for mercy, receive it like a child, and let go of everything to follow Jesus, who is going up to Jerusalem to be killed and to rise, opening blind eyes along the way.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the persistent widow; the Pharisee and the tax collector; receiving the kingdom like a child; the rich ruler and the cost of following; and the third passion prediction with the healing of the blind beggar.

units.label: The persistent widow
units.note: pray at all times and do not lose heart

verses.text: Then Jesus told them a parable about their need to pray at all times and not {{enkakeo|lose heart}}:
“In a certain town there was a judge who neither feared God nor respected men.
And there was a widow in that town who kept appealing to him, ‘Give me justice against my adversary.’
For a while he refused, but later he said to himself, ‘Though I neither fear God nor respect men,
yet because this widow keeps pestering me, I will give her justice. Otherwise, she will wear me out with her perpetual requests.’”
And the Lord said, “Listen to the words of the unjust judge.
Will not God bring about justice for His elect who cry out to Him day and night? Will He delay in helping them?
I tell you, He will promptly carry out justice on their behalf. Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will He find faith on earth?”

units.label: The Pharisee and the tax collector
units.note: God, have mercy on me, a sinner

verses.text: To some who trusted in their own righteousness and viewed others with contempt, He also told this parable:
“Two men went up to the temple to pray. One was a Pharisee and the other a tax collector.
The Pharisee stood by himself and prayed, ‘God, I thank You that I am not like other men, swindlers, evildoers, adulterers, or even like this tax collector.
I fast twice a week and pay tithes of all that I acquire.’
But the tax collector stood at a distance, unwilling even to lift up his eyes to heaven. Instead, he beat his breast and said, ‘God, {{hilaskomai|have mercy}} on me, a sinner!’
I tell you, this man, rather than the Pharisee, went home {{dikaioo|justified}}. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted.”

units.label: Receiving the kingdom like a child
units.note: the kingdom belongs to such as these

verses.text: Now people were even bringing their babies to Jesus for Him to place His hands on them. And when the disciples saw this, they rebuked those who brought them.
But Jesus called the children to Him and said, “Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of God belongs to such as these.
Truly I tell you, anyone who does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will never enter it.”

units.label: The rich ruler and the cost of following
units.note: what is impossible with man is possible with God

verses.text: Then a certain ruler asked Him, “Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?”
“Why do you call Me good?” Jesus replied. “No one is good except God alone.
You know the commandments: ‘Do not commit adultery, do not murder, do not steal, do not bear false witness, honor your father and mother.’”
“All these I have kept from my youth,” he said.
On hearing this, Jesus told him, “You still lack one thing: Sell everything you own and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow Me.”
But when the ruler heard this, he became very sad, because he was extremely wealthy.
Seeing the man’s sadness, Jesus said, “How hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom of God!
Indeed, it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God.”
Those who heard this asked, “Who then can be saved?”
But Jesus said, “What is impossible with man is possible with God.”
“Look,” said Peter, “we have left all we had to follow You.”
“Truly I tell you,” Jesus replied, “no one who has left home or wife or brothers or parents or children for the sake of the kingdom of God
will fail to receive many times more in this age, and in the age to come, eternal life.”

units.label: The passion foretold and the blind beggar
units.note: Son of David, have mercy on me

verses.text: Then Jesus took the Twelve aside and said to them, “Look, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything the prophets have written about the Son of Man will be fulfilled.
He will be delivered over to the Gentiles and will be mocked and insulted and spit upon.
They will flog Him and kill Him, and on the third day He will rise again.”
But the disciples did not understand any of these things. The meaning was hidden from them, and they did not comprehend what He was saying.
As Jesus drew near to Jericho, a blind man was sitting beside the road, begging.
When he heard the crowd going by, he asked what was happening.
“Jesus of Nazareth is passing by,” they told him.
So he called out, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!”
Those who led the way admonished him to be silent, but he cried out all the louder, “Son of David, have mercy on me!”
Jesus stopped and directed that the man be brought to Him. When he had come near, Jesus asked him,
“What do you want Me to do for you?” “Lord,” he said, “let me see again.”
“Receive your sight!” Jesus replied. “Your faith has {{sozo|healed}} you.”
Immediately he received his sight and followed Jesus, glorifying God. And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God.

enkakeo.gloss: To lose heart, to grow weary and give up. Jesus tells the parable of the widow precisely so that His people will pray always and not lose heart. Persistent prayer is not about wearing God down like the unjust judge but about refusing to quit trusting a Father who is nothing like that judge and who loves to answer His crying children.

hilaskomai.gloss: To be merciful, to make atonement, to be propitious. The tax collector's cry is not the ordinary word for mercy but one drawn from the temple's sacrifices: God, be propitiated toward me, the sinner. He pleads not his record but an atonement he cannot make himself, and he goes home justified. It is the prayer of the gospel.

dikaioo.gloss: To justify, to declare righteous. Jesus says the tax collector, not the Pharisee, went home justified, counted righteous before God. The verdict rests not on his works but on God's mercy received by faith, the very heart of how a sinner is set right with God.

sozo.gloss: To save, to heal, to make whole. To the blind beggar who called Jesus Son of David, Jesus says your faith has saved you, and the man both receives his sight and follows in the way. The word joins physical healing to the deeper rescue of the whole person who trusts the Messiah.

basic.context: Jesus tells of a widow who keeps hounding an unjust judge until he grants her justice, and argues from the lesser to the greater: if even that judge yields, how much more will God vindicate His elect who cry to Him. So pray always and do not lose heart. Then two men pray in the temple. The Pharisee thanks God he is not like others and lists his virtues; the tax collector only beats his breast and cries, God, have mercy on me, a sinner. Jesus says the second man went home justified. He welcomes little children as the pattern of receiving the kingdom, and then a rich ruler asks how to inherit eternal life but goes away sad when told to sell everything and follow. It is easier, Jesus says, for a camel to go through a needle's eye than for the rich to be saved, yet what is impossible for man is possible for God. He foretells His death and resurrection a third time, and a blind beggar crying Son of David receives his sight and follows.
basic.hermeneutics: The chapter is bound together by the question of who enters the kingdom and how. The two prayer parables answer it: persistent, humble dependence, not self-confidence. The child, the rich ruler, and the blind beggar illustrate it: those who come with empty hands are received, while those clinging to wealth or merit turn away. Behind it all Jesus is going to Jerusalem to make salvation possible.
basic.originalLanguages: The widow parable is told so we will pray and not enkakeo, lose heart. The tax collector prays hilaskomai, be propitiated toward me, pleading atonement rather than merit, and goes home dikaioo, justified, declared righteous by God. And the blind beggar hears that his faith has sozo him, saved and healed him whole.
basic.typology: The widow crying for justice echoes the persecuted saints crying out to God in the Psalms and Revelation. The tax collector's plea for propitiation points to the temple sacrifice and beyond it to the cross. The blind man given sight fulfills the messianic promise that the Son of David would open blind eyes.
basic.christ: Jesus is the good Teacher who alone is good with God, the One who makes the impossible salvation possible, and the Son of Man going up to Jerusalem to be killed and to rise. He is the Son of David who opens the eyes of the blind, and the One whose mercy the tax collector's cry finally rests upon at the cross.
basic.god: God is the righteous Judge, utterly unlike the unjust one, who swiftly vindicates His crying people. He justifies the humble sinner who begs for mercy and resists the proud who trust themselves. He receives little children and makes possible what no rich man could achieve, for with God nothing is impossible.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 3 declares that God justifies the ungodly by faith. Psalm 51 is the great prayer, have mercy on me, God. Matthew 19 gives the parallel account of the rich young man. Isaiah 35 promises that the eyes of the blind will be opened.
basic.oneStory: On the last stretch to Jerusalem Jesus shows who enters the kingdom: not the self-righteous or the rich in themselves, but those who pray without losing heart, cry for mercy, and come like children. He is going to the cross to do the impossible, to justify sinners, and He opens blind eyes as a sign of the salvation He brings.

context.literary:
Luke 18 is built as a run of reversals, and the order is deliberate. Two parables that Luke alone records open it, and each carries its own introduction telling the reader how to take it: verse 1 says the first is about the need to pray at all times and not lose heart, and verse 9 says the second is aimed at those who trusted in their own righteousness and viewed others with contempt. The first parable is about the long wait for vindication, the second about the posture in which anyone stands before God. Between them they hold persistence and humility together, which is why neither can be turned into a technique.

The middle of the chapter is a chain of entrances. Babies are carried to Jesus and the disciples block them, verses 15 to 17. A ruler walks up with a respectable question and walks away sad, verses 18 to 23. Peter then protests that the Twelve have left everything, verses 28 to 30. Every scene asks the same thing: who gets in, and on what terms? The answer keeps landing on those who bring nothing, the baby, the tax collector, the beggar, while the man with the most to offer leaves. Notice too how the disciples fail in the middle of it: they rebuke the parents in verse 15, they are baffled by the camel saying in verse 26, and verse 34 says three times over that they understood nothing of the passion prediction.

The chapter ends in the same place as its first half began, with a cry. The widow cries for justice, the tax collector cries for mercy, and the beggar cries for mercy again in verses 38 and 39, louder when he is told to be quiet. Between the widow and the beggar sits the one prediction that explains how such cries can be answered, the third announcement of the cross in verses 31 to 33. Luke sets a blind man at the door of Jericho, the last stop before the climb to Jerusalem, so that a sighted crowd who cannot see what lies ahead walks past the one man who sees who is passing.
context.historical:
A widow in the world of the Old Testament stood near the bottom of the social ladder. With no husband to speak for her she depended on the court, and the law gathered her with the orphan and the foreigner as people God Himself defends, Exodus 22:22 to 24 and Deuteronomy 10:18. Judges were commanded to be impartial, Deuteronomy 16:18 to 20, and the prophets complained that the powerful would not take up the widow's case, Isaiah 1:23. A judge who neither feared God nor respected men, verse 2, was therefore the very picture of a court gone wrong, and Jesus' hearers would have known exactly what a woman in her place could and could not do. She had no bribe to offer and no relative to threaten. She had only her voice.

The temple scene is set at the hour of prayer. Two men go up to the temple mount, and the Pharisee's prayer lists practices that exceed what the law asked. The Day of Atonement was the one fast the Torah commanded, Leviticus 16:29 to 31, and he fasts twice a week. He tithes on everything he acquires, going beyond the grain, wine and oil of Deuteronomy 14:22 to 23. Jesus does not mock these practices. The point is that a man can do the right things and still draw the wrong conclusion from them. The tax collector, by contrast, stands for a class that Luke has already shown as a byword for sin, 5:30, 7:34 and 15:1, men who bought the right to collect Roman dues and kept whatever they could add on top, 3:12 to 13.

Babies in verse 15 are brought for a touch of blessing, as Jacob once laid hands on his grandsons, Genesis 48:14. The ruler, archon, is a man of standing, perhaps a synagogue leader, and verse 23 reports that he was extremely wealthy. In a culture that often read prosperity as a sign of God's favour, the disciples' question in verse 26, Who then can be saved?, makes sense: if the man who seemed most blessed cannot get in, who can?

The last scene is on the road from Galilee and the Jordan valley to Jerusalem. Jericho lies far below sea level and the road from it climbs steeply, so verse 31, we are going up to Jerusalem, is meant literally. Pilgrims crowded that road at feast time, and a beggar beside it would have found the best audience of his year.
context.canonical:
The thread that holds the chapter together is an older one: God lifts the lowly and brings down the proud. Hannah sang it, 1 Samuel 2:7 to 8, and Mary sang it in Luke's own opening chapter, 1:52 to 53, so that Luke 18:14, everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, is the same truth now applied to prayer. Jesus uses the saying again in Luke 14:11, and James and Peter pass it on to the church, James 4:6 and 10 and 1 Peter 5:5 to 6, both drawing on Proverbs 3:34.

The cry of the widow has deep roots as well. The unanswered cry of the oppressed is a constant in the Psalms, and the book of Revelation lets the martyrs ask how long before God will judge and avenge, Revelation 6:9 to 10. Luke 18:7, His elect who cry out to Him day and night, is the gospel's reply to that question. The Lord's answer is not that the cry is wrong but that it will be heard, and heard promptly.

The tax collector's plea is the voice of Psalm 51:1, and its verdict is the doctrine Paul will build into Romans and Galatians. Paul uses the verb justify of the sinner who is declared righteous by faith and not by works of the law, Romans 3:28 and Galatians 2:16, and he describes his own former confidence in the flesh, Philippians 3:4 to 9, in terms that read like a commentary on the Pharisee's prayer. That the verdict of Luke 18:14 stands on Jesus' own lips shows that Paul did not invent the idea.

The rich ruler is told by Jesus to follow Him, and Matthew and Mark record the same encounter, Matthew 19:16 to 30 and Mark 10:17 to 31, with the same hard saying about the camel. The question what shall I do to inherit eternal life also appears in Luke 10:25, and there too Jesus points to the commandments. Finally, the blind man's sight is the fulfilment of Isaiah 35:5 and 61:1, the promise Jesus read in the synagogue at Nazareth, Luke 4:18, proclaiming recovery of sight to the blind.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke gathers these scenes to answer a question the church was bound to ask once Jesus had gone: what does it look like to live faithfully while the kingdom has been announced but not yet consummated? Verse 8 holds the key. The vindication of the elect is certain and swift in God's reckoning, yet the Son of Man's question is whether faith will still be found on earth when He comes. Luke wants his readers to keep praying through delay, not because prayer forces God's hand but because prayer is what faith looks like while it waits.

The second parable is aimed at a particular spirit, not at a particular party. Luke says it was told to some who trusted in themselves and despised others, and that is a danger for any people of God, not only first century Pharisees. The shock of the ending is that the man who beat his breast and could not lift his eyes is the one who goes home right with God. Luke intends the reader to feel the offence and then to hear it as good news.

The rich ruler is not told to sell everything because poverty earns heaven. He is told this because he asked what he must do, and the answer exposes what he trusts. Luke wants Theophilus and every reader to see that the one thing lacking is a single allegiance, and that the rest of the chapter, from the child to the beggar, shows what that allegiance looks like in people who have nothing else to hold.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Each parable carries its own instruction, so the prescriptive points are clear: pray at all times and do not lose heart, verse 1, and do not despise others while trusting in your own righteousness, verse 9. Those are meant for us. What is recorded and not commanded are the details of the stories. The judge is not a picture of God's character, as verse 6 makes plain, and the Pharisee's tithing is not condemned as such. We are not told to copy the widow's tactics as if God must be pestered, nor to refuse thanks for God's work in our lives, since thanksgiving as such is not the Pharisee's fault.

The sale of everything in verse 22 is the hardest case. Luke records it as a command to one man, in one encounter, at a moment when the thing he clung to was the thing that stood between him and Jesus. It is not repeated as a rule for every disciple: Zacchaeus in the very next chapter gives half and keeps half, and Jesus calls that salvation, 19:8 to 9. What does carry over is the principle behind the command, that no possession may stand rival to the call to follow Jesus. Where wealth is that rival, the answer is the one Jesus gave. Where it is not, the call is to hold wealth loosely and use it for the poor. The healing of the blind man is a description of what Jesus did, not a promise that every prayer for healing is answered in the same way, though it does show what kind of Lord is being prayed to.

debates.question: Is the widow a picture of how to pray, or a contrast to how God acts?

views.label: A contrast from the lesser to the greater
views.case: Jesus says Listen to the words of the unjust judge, verse 6, and then asks whether God will not bring justice for His elect, verse 7. The argument moves from an unwilling judge to a willing Father. On this reading the widow teaches confidence, not technique: God is not like the judge, so His people can ask without fear of being a nuisance. Most commentators, ancient and modern, take the parable in this way.

views.label: A pattern of persistence
views.case: The introduction in verse 1 says the parable is about the need to pray always and not lose heart, and the widow is the only model of that in the story. Her refusal to give up is what wins the verdict. On this reading God does honour importunity, and the parable promises that those who keep asking will be heard, as in the friend at midnight, Luke 11:5 to 8.

views.label: Both at once
views.case: The parable can use the widow as a pattern and the judge as a foil in the same breath, because the point is not how hard God must be pressed but that those who cry to Him have somewhere to take their cry. Prayer is persistence in the knowledge of a good God, not persistence against a reluctant one.

debates.bearing: Whichever emphasis one prefers, verse 7 settles the question of God's character: He is not the judge. That frees prayer from both despair and manipulation, and it fits Jesus' own habit of praying through long nights before the cross.

debates.question: What does the question about faith in verse 8 mean?

views.label: A warning that faith may be scarce at the end
views.case: Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will He find faith on earth? is read as a sober note that persevering faith is rare, so that delay tests the church. The parable leaves the vindication certain and the endurance uncertain.

views.label: A summons to the kind of faith the widow shows
views.case: The question points back to the pestering widow, so that faith is understood as continued asking. The Son of Man will find it where people keep praying through the delay, and the question is an appeal more than a prediction of failure.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree that the answer is not in the hands of the praying person alone. The disciples are being shaped for the long interval that Luke 19:11 to 27 will go on to describe.

debates.question: Is the command to the ruler for every believer?

views.label: A particular test for a particular man
views.case: Jesus does not say this to Peter, to Zacchaeus or to the women who funded His ministry, Luke 8:3. The command exposes this man's idol, wealth, as the one thing he lacked, and it is not a general entry fee.

views.label: A pattern for every disciple
views.case: Jesus says in Luke 14:33 that anyone who does not renounce all his possessions cannot be His disciple. On this reading the command to the ruler is simply what discipleship always means, with the particular form depending on what holds each person.

debates.bearing: The two readings meet in verse 27: no one can part with what holds him by his own strength, so every disciple, rich or poor, depends on God doing what is impossible.

study.originalLanguages:
The first word to notice is the one in verse 1, enkakeo, usually rendered lose heart. It means to grow weary or to become faint in the face of difficulty, and Paul uses it of not giving up in ministry, 2 Corinthians 4:1 and 16, and of not growing weary in doing good, Galatians 6:9. In Luke 18 it names the real danger of delay: not that God will refuse, but that the one praying will quit.

The judge's final decision in verse 5 uses a vivid verb, hypopiazo, rendered wearing me out. Its root sense is to strike under the eye, to give a black eye. Paul uses it of disciplining his own body, 1 Corinthians 9:27. The judge's joke on himself is that this small widow might yet bruise him. The justice she asks for in verses 3, 5 and 7 comes from ekdikeo and ekdikesis, a word group that covers vindication and also vengeance. It describes a court putting wrong right, and it is the same word that Luke 21:22 will use for the days of judgment on Jerusalem. The sentence in verse 7 that God will not defer is translated from a verb related to makrothymeo, the word for patience or long suffering, James 5:7 to 8. Translators differ on whether God is said to be patient with the elect or slow toward them. The more natural sense is that He will not be slow, which verse 8 confirms with the word promptly.

In the temple parable, the Pharisee stood pros heauton, and the Greek can mean either that he stood by himself or that he prayed to himself, which is why translations vary. Either way, his prayer is a catalogue of self, with the word I at its centre. The tax collector's prayer in verse 13 uses hilaskomai, a verb that appears in the New Testament only here and in Hebrews 2:17, where Christ makes propitiation for the sins of the people. It belongs to the language of the mercy seat, and the related noun hilasterion in Romans 3:25 names the place of atonement. His plea is therefore much more than a request for leniency: he asks to be covered, the way the atonement cover covered the ark. He also calls himself, literally, the sinner, with the definite article, as though no other were in view. The verb in verse 14, dedikaiomenos, is a perfect participle, justified with a standing that continues, which is how Paul will use it.

In verse 15 Luke says people brought brephe, babies or infants, where Matthew and Mark say paidia, children. Luke's word underlines how helpless those are whom Jesus says the kingdom belongs to. In verse 17 the phrase receive the kingdom like a little child can be read two ways: receive it as a child receives, or receive it as one receives a child. The first fits the context of helplessness and gift best.

Verse 25 uses belone for the needle in Luke, where Matthew and Mark use a different word. The saying is deliberately absurd, and its force lies in the impossibility, which the disciples understand in verse 26. And finally the verb sozo, to save or make whole, links three scenes: the crowd asks in verse 26 who then can be saved, using sozo, and Jesus tells the blind man in verse 42 that his faith has saved him, the same verb the BSB renders has healed you. In Luke 19:10 the Son of Man comes to save the lost. The same word is thus used for the healing of a body and the rescue of a soul, and Luke does not separate them.

typology.type: The persecuted who cry out, Luke 18:7
typology.fulfillment: The picture of the elect crying day and night echoes every psalm of lament and the souls under the altar in Revelation 6:9 to 10, who ask how long before God judges. Jesus answers that the delay is not neglect, and He is Himself the Judge who will act, Acts 17:31. The escalation is that in Christ the cry is no longer addressed to a distant court: the Son of Man whom the elect await is the One who has already borne injustice, Isaiah 53:7 to 8, and will return to set all things right. The type falls short because the widow persuades an unwilling man, while the elect are heard by a Father who loves them, Luke 11:13.

typology.type: The tax collector and the mercy seat, Luke 18:13
typology.fulfillment: The tax collector pleads for hilaskomai, the verb that belongs to the mercy seat where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement, Leviticus 16:14 to 15. He is in the temple, where sacrifices were made, but he asks for what the sacrifices pointed to. Paul says God put forward Christ Jesus as a propitiation by His blood, Romans 3:25, and Hebrews 2:17 says Christ became a merciful and faithful high priest to make propitiation for the sins of the people. The fulfilment is that the atoning work this man could only ask for has now been done once for all, Hebrews 9:12. The type falls short because the temple altar had to be approached again and again, while Christ's offering does not.

typology.type: The child and the kingdom, Luke 18:16 to 17
typology.fulfillment: A child comes with nothing, trusts a parent and receives what is given. The pattern appears in Psalm 131:2, where the psalmist stills his soul like a weaned child, and Isaiah 11:6 speaks of a little child leading in the peaceable kingdom. Jesus makes this the mark of everyone who enters, Matthew 18:3. Paul extends it to adoption, Romans 8:15, where believers receive the Spirit of sonship and cry Abba. The escalation is from a posture to a status: those who receive like children become children of God. The pattern falls short if it is read as childish innocence, for the point here is dependence and not virtue.

typology.type: The blind man at Jericho, Luke 18:35 to 43
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah promised that the eyes of the blind would be opened when God came to save, Isaiah 35:5, and Jesus claimed the promise in Nazareth, Luke 4:18. The healing at the gate of Jericho is a sign of that age arriving. It has a second layer in the story: the disciples cannot understand the passion prediction in verse 34, but the blind man sees who Jesus is and follows. Paul says the god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, 2 Corinthians 4:4, and that God has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of His glory in the face of Christ, 2 Corinthians 4:6. The physical healing points to a deeper sight, and it falls short of it because the man he was could still lose his eyes again.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ by the contrast between two kinds of prayer. The Pharisee's prayer rests on what he has done, and the tax collector's rests on what someone else must do for him. Jesus does not leave that mercy as an abstraction. He is on the way to Jerusalem to be the one in whom God answers the tax collector's cry, and verses 31 to 33 describe how: the Son of Man will be delivered over to the Gentiles, mocked, insulted, spat upon, flogged and killed, and on the third day He will rise. Luke gives this prediction right after the hardest saying about salvation, so the reader is meant to see the answer to the question Who then can be saved? The impossible thing that God makes possible is carried out on the cross.

The ruler's question exposes a second Christ theme. He calls Jesus good Teacher, and Jesus asks why, since no one is good except God alone. This is not a denial of His own goodness. It is a challenge: if you say I am good, do you know what you are saying? The ruler is invited to follow Him, the invitation that Peter, Levi and the Twelve have already accepted, and the whole chapter says that to follow Jesus is to find what eternal life is. Peter's claim that the disciples have left everything draws a promise in verses 29 and 30 that no one who leaves home for the kingdom will fail to receive far more in this age and eternal life in the age to come, and the one making the promise is the One who has Himself no place to lay His head, Luke 9:58.

Jesus is also the Son of David in the blind man's mouth. The title is royal and messianic, from the promise to David in 2 Samuel 7:12 to 16, and the blind man recognises it when the sighted crowd does not. Jesus does not silence the cry. He stops, summons the man and asks what he wants, which is the question God asks every time a person comes. The reply Receive your sight is a word of authority of the kind only the messianic King can speak, and the healing makes the same point as the miracles Jesus listed for John the Baptist's disciples, Luke 7:22.

Finally, the little children point to Him as well. He is the one through whom the kingdom is received as a gift, and He is the Son who received everything from the Father, Luke 10:22. Paul says that in Christ we are no longer slaves but sons, Galatians 4:4 to 7. The caution is that the widow's judge is not Christ and the Pharisee is not simply a villain. The Gospel does not force every detail of the parables into a picture of Jesus. It lets them each make their own point and then sets Jesus at the centre of the chapter as the one who answers all its questions: who can be saved, who is good, who is the Son of David, and who will bring justice.
study.god:
The unjust judge is introduced to show what God is not. The argument in verses 6 to 8 is made of two questions that expect the answer yes: will God not bring about justice, and will He continue to defer? He is the Judge who neither lacks fear of God nor respect for people, because He is God and respects no person for status, Deuteronomy 10:17 to 18. He is also the God who is near to His people, and verse 8 says He will promptly carry out justice, which means that what looks like delay from our side is not slowness from His. Peter says the same thing in the other direction, that the Lord is not slow in keeping His promise but patient, 2 Peter 3:9. The two truths hold together: justice is certain, and its timing is in a patience that gives people time to repent.

The tax collector's prayer shows God as the one who justifies. He does not weigh the two men on a scale and find the tax collector slightly less bad. The verdict in verse 14 is that this man goes home justified rather than the other. That is the word of a judge giving a declaration. The mercy asked for is received, and it is received because God Himself provides the covering, as the verb hilaskomai implies. In the Old Testament, God says He will have compassion on whom He will have compassion, Exodus 33:19, and Isaiah 57:15 says He dwells with the contrite and lowly. Luke 18 shows that the high and holy God lives with the one who beats his breast.

The saying to the ruler, no one is good except God alone, brings out the holiness of God. Goodness in the full sense belongs to Him, and everyone else is good only by derivation. That is why the commandments Jesus lists cannot rescue the man: the man keeps them, he thinks, but he has not seen that they presuppose a God who is the only good. It is also a hint that the One who is addressed as good is more than a teacher.

The saying in verse 27 is a statement about divine power: what is impossible with man is possible with God. It echoes the reply to Abraham and Sarah, Is anything too difficult for the LORD?, Genesis 18:14, Jeremiah 32:17 and Gabriel's word to Mary, Luke 1:37. God is not only able to do hard things. He is able to do the thing that no human strength can do, which is to change a heart that holds on to wealth, or to give life to the dead. The passion prediction is where that power is exercised.

For worship, these truths shape the way we come. We come as the widow does, sure of a Judge who will answer. We come as the tax collector does, with no claim but mercy. We come as the child does, with open hands, and as the blind man does, naming what we need and calling Him by His true name. The God of Luke 18 is approached best by those who know that they cannot come in any other way.

crossReferences.note: The friend at midnight is the other prayer parable in Luke, and it too turns on boldness. The man gets up because of his friend's shameless asking, not because of friendship. Jesus then moves at once to the Father who gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask, 11:13. Read together with Luke 18, the two parables teach that persistence is welcome and that the One addressed is far kinder than the sleeper or the judge.

Abraham asks, Will not the Judge of all the earth do right? Luke 18:7 asks the same of the Judge of the elect. The patriarch's question is the root of the confidence in the widow parable: God's justice is not arbitrary or slow, and those who lay their case before Him are asking something He has bound Himself to do.

Any widow who cries to God will be heard, and God warns that His anger will burn against those who oppress her. This is the background against which the widow of Luke 18 is vulnerable and also the reason her cry cannot fail. The law presents God as her defender long before the parable pictures a judge who will not hear her.

David's cry for mercy after Bathsheba is the model of the tax collector's prayer. Like him, David has no defence and asks for mercy according to God's steadfast love. The psalm teaches that such a plea is received, since the sacrifices God wants are a broken spirit and a contrite heart, verse 17. Luke 18:14 shows that promise being honoured.

Paul was a Pharisee who could count a long list of reasons for confidence, and he counts them as loss for the sake of Christ. He wants a righteousness that comes through faith in Christ, not his own from the law. This is the Pharisee's prayer turned inside out by someone who lived it, and it shows how Luke 18:9 to 14 became the standing doctrine of the apostolic church.

Ten lepers cry Jesus, Master, have mercy on us, using the same verb as the blind man in 18:38. The one who returns is a Samaritan, and Jesus says his faith has saved him. The two stories bracket the second half of the journey to Jerusalem with outsiders who cry for mercy and receive it, while insiders miss it.

Mark tells of the same rich man, adds that Jesus looked at him and loved him, verse 21, and notes that Jesus looked around before saying how hard it is for the rich to enter, verse 23. Reading Mark's detail beside Luke shows that the command to sell everything was spoken in love and not in contempt. It is also the same Jesus who then says that for God all things are possible.

The disciples ask who is greatest and Jesus sets a child among them, telling them that unless they change and become like children they will never enter. The point is the same as Luke 18:17 but the setting is a dispute about status, which shows how persistently the Twelve needed correcting.

When God comes to save, the eyes of the blind will be opened and the lame will leap. The blind man at Jericho is one of the signs that the promised day has come. Isaiah 35 also speaks of a highway for the redeemed, and the blind man who follows Jesus in glory to God, Luke 18:43, is the first to walk it.

Paul says the Lord Jesus Christ, though rich, became poor for your sake so that through His poverty you might become rich. This is the answer to the ruler's sadness. The One who asks him to give up wealth has Himself given up far more, and the treasure in heaven that He offers is real because He is its source.

The prophet's Servant offers His back to those who strike and does not hide His face from insult and spitting. Luke 18:32 speaks of the Son of Man being mocked, insulted and spat upon, so the third prediction of the passion reads Isaiah's Servant onto the Son of Man. Jesus tells the Twelve that everything the prophets have written will be fulfilled, 18:31, and this is one of the passages in mind.

study.oneStory:
The question of who may stand before God is as old as Eden. Adam and Eve were made to live in trusting dependence, receiving the garden as gift, and the fall of Genesis 3 was a grasping after what God had not given. Every figure in Luke 18 stands somewhere on that map. The Pharisee has taken up the posture of the man who has made himself, and the ruler clings to what he has built. The widow, the tax collector, the children and the beggar are those who have nothing and ask, and God receives them. The chapter does not invent that order. It restores it.

The Old Testament had been preparing for this verdict all along. The patriarchs lived by promise, Abraham was counted righteous by believing, Genesis 15:6, and Israel was told that it was chosen not because of its size or goodness, Deuteronomy 7:7 to 8. The prophets cried to God for justice for the widow and the orphan, and promised a day when the blind would see. The Psalms train the people to cry for mercy. Luke 18 picks up all these threads in a single journey to Jerusalem.

The word elect in verse 7 draws the people of God back to the one chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world, Ephesians 1:4. God's elect are not a spiritual elite but those who have been rescued, and the Lord's concern is for their cry. The promise of verse 8 that vindication is coming links to the whole biblical hope that God will judge the world with righteousness, Psalm 96:13, and finally set right all that has gone wrong.

The passion prediction in verses 31 to 33 is the hinge in the larger story. Everything the prophets wrote about the Son of Man is to be fulfilled in the going up to Jerusalem, and the disciples cannot see it. That is why the blind man matters: the story of redemption depends on God opening eyes. After the resurrection Jesus will open the Scriptures and the minds of the disciples, Luke 24:27 and 45, and the road to Emmaus completes what the road to Jericho begins.

The story ends in the new creation. In the age to come, verse 30, the promise of eternal life is fulfilled. Revelation 21 pictures a city where there is no more crying and the Judge makes everything new, and Revelation 22:4 says that His servants will see His face. The widow's cry is answered in full, the tax collector's debt is gone, the child is at home, the ruler's wealth is no longer a rival, and every blind eye sees. Until then the people of God pray without losing heart, because the end of the story is already sure.

quiz.q: What is the main point of the parable of the persistent widow?

options.text: Keep praying and do not lose heart, for the righteous God will surely vindicate His people.
options.note: Luke 18:1,7-8 states the parable's aim: pray always, do not lose heart, God will bring justice.

options.text: Persistent prayer eventually wins what we ask for.
options.note: Persistence is commended, but the point is God's faithfulness, not wearing Him down like the judge.

options.text: God is reluctant, so we must pester Him until He acts.
options.note: The argument is from the lesser to the greater; God is utterly unlike the unwilling judge.

options.text: Justice comes only to those who shout the loudest.
options.note: The parable assures God's elect of vindication, not the loudest of a reward for volume.

quiz.q: Why did the tax collector, rather than the Pharisee, go home justified?

options.text: Because he abandoned every claim and simply begged God for mercy as a sinner.
options.note: Luke 18:13-14 shows justification resting on humble mercy received, not merit.

options.text: Because he humbled himself while the Pharisee exalted himself.
options.note: True to the closing line, but it omits the specific plea for mercy that is the ground.

options.text: Because he had committed fewer sins than the Pharisee.
options.note: He confesses he is a sinner; his justification is by mercy, not by a better record.

options.text: Because he fasted and tithed more faithfully.
options.note: That describes the Pharisee's boast; the tax collector pleaded only for mercy.

quiz.q: What does Jesus mean by welcoming the little children?

options.text: The kingdom must be received like a child, with empty-handed dependence, or it cannot be entered.
options.note: Luke 18:16-17 makes childlike reception the pattern for entering the kingdom.

options.text: Children are especially precious to Jesus.
options.note: True and shown, but the teaching point is how the kingdom must be received.

options.text: Disciples should be gentle and welcoming to children.
options.note: A fair application, but Jesus is teaching about receiving the kingdom, not mainly about hospitality.

options.text: Only literal children can enter the kingdom of God.
options.note: Jesus says adults must receive it like children, not that only children may enter.

quiz.q: What does the rich ruler's departure and Jesus' saying reveal?

options.text: Wealth can hold the heart's throne, making salvation impossible for man but possible with God.
options.note: Luke 18:24-27 exposes the danger of riches and points to God alone as able to save.

options.text: It is very hard for the rich to enter the kingdom of God.
options.note: True, but it omits the hope that what is impossible with man is possible with God.

options.text: Rich people are excluded from the kingdom.
options.note: Jesus says it is hard, not impossible; with God even a rich person can be saved.

options.text: Keeping the commandments from youth is enough to inherit eternal life.
options.note: The ruler claimed this, yet still lacked the one thing and turned away.

quiz.q: How does the blind beggar respond to Jesus near Jericho?

options.text: He cries out all the louder to the Son of David for mercy, receives his sight, and follows Jesus.
options.note: Luke 18:38-43 shows persistent faith, healing, and discipleship.

options.text: He asks Jesus for mercy and is given his sight.
options.note: True, but it omits his refusal to be silenced and his following Jesus afterward.

options.text: He waits quietly until Jesus notices him.
options.note: The opposite: he shouted and would not be hushed by the crowd.

options.text: He is silenced by the crowd and misses his chance.
options.note: He cried out all the louder and was healed.

questions: Jesus told the widow's parable so we would pray and not lose heart. Where have you quietly given up praying because the answer has been long in coming?
The tax collector could only say, God, have mercy on me, a sinner. Is your confidence before God built on your own record or on His mercy received?
The Pharisee measured himself against other people. Whom are you tempted to look down on, and how does that expose a trust in your own righteousness?
The rich ruler kept the rules but could not let go of his wealth. What is the one thing you are clinging to that Jesus may be asking you to release in order to follow Him?
The blind beggar would not be silenced. Is there a cry for mercy you have muffled because others told you to be quiet or because you felt unworthy to shout?

translationNotes.note: A footnote notes the phrase may read 'stood and prayed to himself', fitting his self-absorbed prayer.

The tax collector's cry uses a word tied to atonement, literally 'be propitiated toward me, the sinner'. He does not merely ask for leniency but pleads for God to deal with him on the basis of a covering sacrifice, language fulfilled at the cross.
The promise assures that whatever is left for the kingdom is repaid many times over now and with eternal life to come.
